problem: The title is an image or a sign the narrator reads, and every chorus says the same thing.
technique: Write the title as an unfinished frame: a thing the narrator reads, plus 'tells me' or 'says', plus a verdict. Keep the frame words fixed and change the verdict. Give it a hopeful completion first, as the last line of a verse, then the final completion as the last line of the chorus, so the same words deliver opposite conclusions.
example: Paraphrase: in Zach Bryan's 'Something in the Orange', the title phrase first lands at the end of verse 2, completed with hope that the couple aren't finished; each chorus ends with the same frame completed with the verdict that she isn't coming back. The colour itself is never explained.
limits: Title positions and completions come from a fetch tool's description of a lyric display whose licence was not shown, corroborated by an analyst's guide; text-only, not checked against the recording; no writer statement about the device.
when_not: If the hopeful completion is cut or buried mid-verse, the device disappears and the chorus is just a sad line. A frame with nothing concrete to read ('something tells me') is a cliché; the reading needs an object, such as a colour, a light or a sound.
distinct_from: C31: keeps one phrase's two readings open; here the readings are stated one after the other as different completions of a fixed frame
C47: withholds an arrival; here nothing is withheld, the verdict flips
C25: moves the blame; here the verdict on the relationship moves

problem: The title phrase's everyday meaning will mislead on first hearing, and the room can't decide whether to hide it, explain it or change it.
technique: State the phrase plainly in the first line, as an admission. Let the chorus give the reason: a plain line, addressed to the real object of the feeling, that explains the opening without contradicting it, so the turn is an explanation, not a trick. Choose the reading that makes the phrase's everyday sense partly true, pushed to an extreme. Before polishing, play it to one outside listener with one question: does it make sense?
example: Paraphrase: 'Girl Crush' opens on its title as a confession and lists the other woman's lips, perfume, hair and touch. The chorus, the first section to address the man, explains that she wants to be the other woman so he would want her. The writers sent the voice memo to their publisher asking only whether it made sense; their worry was whether the jealousy would be understood.
limits: The does-it-make-sense check and the writers' worry are documented (SC-S1, tool-extracted). The structure comes from a tool's description of a press page's lyric block (licence not shown) and a review. The 'explanation payoff' framing is the analyst's. Lexical; no audio needed.
when_not: Where an audience may stop at the opening (radio skims, a short clip), a turn that lives in the chorus may never be heard: 'Girl Crush' drew complaints from listeners who heard a different song, and the label filmed an explainer. If the 'misreading' would be welcome to the artist or audience, there is nothing to explain.
distinct_from: C30: choose the angle that turns the phrase; this card is about where and how the turn lands (opening statement, chorus reason)
C31: keep two readings open; this card settles them
C29: reverse an idiom's charge; here the everyday sense is pushed to an extreme, not reversed

problem: A recurring image (a colour, a light, an object) is just decoration; it means the same thing each time it comes back.
technique: Give the image a new source each time it returns (natural light, then artificial light, then something leaving), and make each move coincide with a change in what the narrator believes. Never explain the image; let where it is attached do the work.
example: Paraphrase: in 'Something in the Orange' the colour is attached in turn to evening or morning sun, a bulb seen in the lover's eyes, headlights, and in the last stanza light falling on everything around the narrator. An analyst reads it moving from lingering hope to a harsh bulb to loss and anger.
limits: Two text-only descriptions (a fetch tool's description of a display with no licence shown, and an analyst's guide) that disagree on which verse holds which light; no writer statement; not checked against the recording.
when_not: The analyst's own caveat: if listeners miss the shifts, the image reads as vague and the title as unexplained. In a fast, dense lyric the moves may not register; a song that needs one fixed anchor image (C23) should keep it fixed.
distinct_from: C23: one concrete anchor image for an unnamed addressee; here the image moves
C33: promote a concrete noun to the title; this is about how a recurring image changes after it is chosen
C11: one petty, checkable detail; here a single image recurs with a changing source
